q: What is the major product when 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is treated with NaOCH<sub>3</sub> in methanol?
h: Tertiary substrate plus a strong base: which mechanisms are possible?
w: A 3° carbon cannot undergo SN2, and methoxide is a strong base, so E2 dominates: 2-methylpropene.
x: tert-Butyl methyl ether would need S<sub>N</sub>2 at a 3° carbon (blocked) or S<sub>N</sub>1 solvolysis, which is far slower than E2 with a strong base present.
Isobutyl methyl ether has the oxygen on a different carbon; nothing here moves the reaction site.
No water is present, so tert-butyl alcohol cannot form.

q: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane is dissolved in methanol at 25 °C with no added base. What happens mainly?
c: S<sub>N</sub>1, giving mainly tert-butyl methyl ether (with some 2-methylpropene by E1)
S<sub>N</sub>2, giving mainly tert-butyl methyl ether
E1, giving mainly 2-methylpropene (with some ether by S<sub>N</sub>1)
h: Methanol is a weak nucleophile and weak base in a polar protic solvent. What does a 3° bromide do there at room temperature?
w: With no strong base, the 3° bromide ionizes in the polar protic solvent (solvolysis). The carbocation is captured mostly by solvent at 25 °C: SN1 gives mainly tert-butyl methyl ether, with a smaller amount of 2-methylpropene from E1. Heating would increase the alkene fraction.
x: E2 needs a strong base; methanol is far too weak a base for E2 to compete with ionization.
A 3° carbon is too hindered for backside attack; the ether forms by S<sub>N</sub>1, not S<sub>N</sub>2.
At room temperature, capture of the carbocation by the solvent beats loss of a proton; E1 is the minor path.

q: (R)-2-Bromobutane is treated with NaN3 in DMSO. What is the major product?
h: Azide is an excellent nucleophile but a weak base, and DMSO is polar aprotic.
w: N3− is a strong nucleophile and weak base, and DMSO leaves it unsolvated, so a 2° bromide reacts by SN2 with backside attack and inversion: (S)-2-azidobutane. (N3 and Br both have top priority, so inversion changes R to S here.)
x: Retention would need front-side attack; S<sub>N</sub>2 goes with inversion of configuration.
Azide is a weak base (HN<sub>3</sub> pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 4.7), so E2 to 2-butene is minor.
1-Butene would need a strong, bulky base; azide gives substitution.

q: 2-Bromopentane is heated with NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol at 55 °C. What is the major product?
h: A 2° halide with a strong, small base and heat: substitution or elimination? Then pick the alkene.
w: With a 2° halide, a strong base such as ethoxide (and heat) favors E2 over SN2. Small bases give the Zaitsev alkene, and of the two 2-pentenes the trans isomer is formed faster (less steric strain in its transition state): (E)-2-pentene.
x: The S<sub>N</sub>2 ether forms, but with a 2° halide, a strong base and heat it is the minor product.
1-Pentene is the Hofmann product; ethoxide is small, so the more substituted 2-pentene dominates.
(Z)-2-Pentene forms in smaller amount; its anti-periplanar conformer puts the alkyl groups gauche.

q: 1-Bromobutane is treated separately with (I) NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol and (II) (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COK in tert-butyl alcohol. What is the main product in each case?
h: A primary carbon is easy to attack from the back. Which base is too bulky to act as a nucleophile?
w: With an unhindered 1° bromide, ethoxide acts mainly as a nucleophile (SN2), giving 1-ethoxybutane. tert-Butoxide is too bulky to reach the carbon, so it removes a β H instead (E2), giving 1-butene.
x: Ethoxide with an unhindered 1° bromide gives mainly S<sub>N</sub>2; E2 is minor.
tert-Butoxide is a poor nucleophile because of its bulk; with a 1° bromide it gives mainly E2.
2-Butene cannot form directly from 1-bromobutane by E2; the C=C must include C1, which bore the Br.

q: Which reagent converts bromocyclohexane mainly into a substitution product?
h: For a 2° substrate you need a nucleophile that is strong but only weakly basic.
w: Secondary substrates give E2 with strong bases and SN2 with good nucleophiles that are weak bases. CH3S− in DMF (polar aprotic) is highly nucleophilic but much less basic than alkoxides, so it gives cyclohexyl methyl sulfide by SN2.
x: Methoxide is a strong base; with a 2° ring halide and heat it gives mainly cyclohexene by E2.
tert-Butoxide is a strong, bulky base that gives E2 (cyclohexene).
DBU is a non-nucleophilic amidine base used specifically to promote E2.

q: Which combination is the best way to prepare tert-butyl ethyl ether, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: The Williamson synthesis is S<sub>N</sub>2. Which partner must be the alkyl halide?
w: The C–O bond must be made by SN2, so the halide must be unhindered. tert-Butoxide + bromoethane works: a 1° bromide with no β-branching undergoes SN2 readily. Putting the halogen on the 3° carbon makes the alkoxide act as a base and gives 2-methylpropene by E2.
x: Ethoxide with a 3° bromide gives E2 (2-methylpropene), because the 3° carbon cannot undergo backside attack.
Changing the solvent or leaving group does not help: the 3° chloride still cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2, and ethoxide eliminates.
A neutral alcohol is a weak nucleophile; without converting it to the alkoxide, S<sub>N</sub>2 on bromoethane is extremely slow.

q: Which reaction gives mainly an elimination product?
h: Classify each substrate (1° or 2°) and each reagent (strong base, good nucleophile/weak base, or weak nucleophile/weak base).
w: 2-Bromopropane with ethoxide and heat: a 2° substrate with a strong base gives mainly E2 (propene, roughly 80%). The 1° bromide with ethoxide gives mainly SN2; cyanide in DMSO is a good nucleophile and weaker base, so the 2° bromide gives SN2; in ethanol with no base at room temperature, the slow solvolysis gives mainly the ether.
x: A 1° unhindered bromide gives mainly S<sub>N</sub>2 with ethoxide; E2 is minor.
Cyanide is a good nucleophile and much weaker base than ethoxide, and DMSO speeds S<sub>N</sub>2; substitution dominates.
Ethanol alone is a weak base; solvolysis of a 2° bromide at room temperature gives mainly substitution, not alkene.

q:
Assign the main mechanism to each reaction.
I. (S)-2-iodooctane + NaCN, DMSO
II. 2-bromo-2-methylpentane in 80% aqueous acetone, 25 °C
III. 2-bromo-2-methylpentane + NaOCH2CH3, ethanol, heat
c: I S<sub>N</sub>2; II S<sub>N</sub>1; III E2
I S<sub>N</sub>2; II E1; III S<sub>N</sub>1
I S<sub>N</sub>1; II S<sub>N</sub>1; III E1
I E2; II S<sub>N</sub>1; III S<sub>N</sub>2
h: Match substrate class with reagent strength: good nucleophile/weak base, weak nucleophile/weak base, strong base.
w: I: a 2° iodide with a strong nucleophile/weak base in a polar aprotic solvent: SN2 with inversion. II: a 3° bromide in a polar protic solvent with only water as nucleophile at room temperature: ionization, mainly SN1 (some E1). III: the same 3° bromide with a strong base and heat: E2. Answer: I SN2; II SN1; III E2.
x: A 3° substrate with a strong base (III) gives E2, not S<sub>N</sub>1; and II at 25 °C gives mainly substitution.
I has a strong nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent, which favors S<sub>N</sub>2, and III has a strong base, which makes it E2, not E1.
Cyanide is a weak base and a 2° iodide is not hindered enough for E2 to win; S<sub>N</sub>2 dominates. A 3° carbon cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2.

q: For a 2° alkyl bromide with ethoxide, raising the temperature increases the fraction of alkene relative to ether. Which explanation is best?
c: Elimination forms more molecules, so its ΔS is more positive and the −TΔS term matters more at high temperature
Elimination has the lower activation energy, so heating speeds it up more than substitution
At high temperature the ether product is converted into the alkene
Heating makes ethoxide a weaker base and a stronger nucleophile
h: Count the particles on each side for substitution and for elimination.
w: Substitution: 2 reactants → 2 products. Elimination: 2 reactants → 3 products (alkene, alcohol, halide). Elimination has a more positive ΔS, so ΔG = ΔH − TΔS becomes more favorable for elimination as T rises; heating therefore increases the alkene fraction.
x: Heating helps the reaction with the higher barrier more, not the lower one; elimination generally has the higher barrier and is the one helped.
Ethers are stable to ethoxide; the ether does not convert to alkene under these conditions.
Temperature does not turn ethoxide into a better nucleophile; if anything, the elimination pathway gains.

q: What is the IUPAC name of this compound?
h: The C=C carbons are C1 and C2. Then choose the direction that gives the lowest set of substituent locants.
w: The double bond must be C1=C2. Starting at the methyl-bearing alkene carbon (C1) and going through C2 puts the other methyl at C5: {1,5}. Starting at the other alkene carbon gives {2,4}. Compare at the first point of difference: 1 < 2, so the name is 1,5-dimethylcyclohexene.
x: {2,4} loses to {1,5} at the first point of difference (1 < 2).
1,3-Dimethylcyclohexene would have the second methyl on the carbon right after C2; here two CH<sub>2</sub> groups separate them going that way.
Locants 3 and 5 would place both methyls off the double bond; one methyl is on an alkene carbon.

q: What is the IUPAC name of this alkene?
h: Two five-carbon chains contain the C=C; choose the one with more substituents. Then rank the two groups on C3 by CIP.
w: Chains through the ethyl or through the isopropyl both have five carbons; the one through the isopropyl carries two substituents (ethyl and methyl), so the parent is 3-ethyl-4-methylpent-2-ene. For E/Z: on C2, CH3 > H; on C3, isopropyl (C,C,H) > ethyl (C,H,H). The C2 methyl and the isopropyl are on the same side, so the name is (Z)-3-ethyl-4-methylpent-2-ene.
x: Isopropyl outranks ethyl at the first atom (C,C,H vs C,H,H); it is cis to the C2 methyl, which is Z.
The E/Z label is right, but when two chains are equally long, the parent is the one with more substituents (two vs one).
Both the parent chain and the E/Z label are wrong.

h: Rank the two groups on each alkene carbon by atomic number. Do not judge by where the methyl groups are.
w: On C2, Cl (Z = 17) > CH3; on C3, CH3 > H. Z means Cl and the C3 methyl are on the same side, so the two methyl groups are trans to each other. The structure with Cl cis to the C3 methyl (methyls trans) is (Z)-2-chloro-2-butene.
x: Here Cl and the C3 methyl are on opposite sides: this is the E isomer, even though the two methyls look cis.
This is (Z)-1-chloro-2-butene; the Cl is on C1, not on an alkene carbon.
This is 2-chloro-1-butene, which has two H on C1 and no E/Z isomers.

q: Which alkene can exist as E and Z isomers?
h: Each alkene carbon needs two different groups.
w: 3-Methylpent-2-ene: C2 has CH3 and H, and C3 has CH3 and CH2CH3, so both alkene carbons carry two different groups and E/Z isomers exist.
x: In 2-methylpent-2-ene, C2 carries two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups, so no E/Z isomers exist.
In 3-ethylpent-2-ene, C3 carries two identical ethyl groups, so no E/Z isomers exist.
In 2-methylpent-1-ene, C1 is =CH<sub>2</sub> with two H atoms, so no E/Z isomers exist.

q: (3R,4S)-3-Bromo-4-methylhexane is heated with NaOCH2CH3 in ethanol. What is the major product?
h: First pick the Zaitsev carbon. It has one H, so the anti-periplanar conformation fixes the alkene geometry.
w: Ethoxide is small, so the trisubstituted C3=C4 alkene (Zaitsev) is major. C4 has a single H, so only one conformer has it anti to Br. In that conformer the C3 ethyl is gauche to the C4 ethyl, so they become cis. Priorities: on C3, ethyl > H; on C4, ethyl > methyl. Higher priorities on the same side: (Z)-3-methylhex-3-ene. The (3R,4R) diastereomer would give the E alkene.
x: The E isomer comes from the (3R,4R)/(3S,4S) diastereomer; E2 from this isomer gives only Z.
4-Methylhex-2-ene comes from loss of a C2 hydrogen; it is only disubstituted and is minor with a small base.
The S<sub>N</sub>2 product (with inversion at C3) is minor: the 2° carbon is next to a branch point, and a strong base with heat favors E2.

q: Which alkyl bromide gives a single alkene (no constitutional or E/Z isomers) on E2 with NaOCH2CH3?
h: List every β carbon with H and the alkene each would give; then check each for E/Z.
w: In 3-bromo-3-ethylpentane the three β carbons are equivalent CH2 groups, and each gives CH3CH=C(CH2CH3)2, 3-ethylpent-2-ene. Its C3 bears two identical ethyl groups, so it has no E/Z isomers: a single product.
x: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane gives both 2-methyl-2-butene and 2-methyl-1-butene.
3-Bromo-3-methylpentane gives (E)- and (Z)-3-methylpent-2-ene plus 2-ethylbut-1-ene.
2-Bromo-3-methylbutane gives 2-methyl-2-butene and 3-methyl-1-butene.
